concept.title: The Thermodynamics of Sorting: Entropy and Computational Work
concept.concept_description: Sorting a list of n elements reduces the entropy from log(n!) bits to 0 bits, doing thermodynamic work W = kT * log(n!) in the process. But this is only true if sorting is irreversible — if the sorted list uniquely determines the input, then sorting is reversible and does no thermodynamic work. The key insight: comparison-based sorting makes irreversible comparisons (you learn a < b but discard the possibility a > b), and each comparison reduces entropy by at most 1 bit. So n*log(n) comparisons reduce entropy by at most n*log(n) bits, which matches log(n!) ~ n*log(n) bits. Conjecture: the minimum thermodynamic work of sorting n elements is W_min = kT * log(n!), and this work is achieved by optimal comparison-based sorting algorithms (merge sort, heapsort). Sub-optimal algorithms (bubble sort: n^2 comparisons) do more thermodynamic work than necessary: W_bubble = kT * n^2, wasting kT * (n^2 - n*log(n)) bits of entropy reduction. Conjecture: any sorting algorithm that makes C(n) comparisons does thermodynamic work proportional to C(n) * kT, and the optimal work is W_min = kT * n*log(n) (Stirling's approximation). Test: simulate sorting algorithms with entropy bookkeeping, verify W = kT * log(n!) for merge sort and W = kT * n^2 for bubble sort. Impact: sorting is a thermodynamic process. The n*log(n) lower bound is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics.

import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph Finset

/-! ## The friendship graph -/

/-- Adjacency of the friendship graph `F_n` on vertex set `Option (Fin n × Bool)`.
The centre is `none`; the two outer vertices of triangle `i` are `some (i, false)` and
`some (i, true)`.  The centre is adjacent to every outer vertex, and the two outer vertices of a
common triangle are adjacent to each other; there are no other edges. -/
def frAdj (n : ℕ) (x y : Option (Fin n × Bool)) : Prop :=
  match x, y with
  | none, none => False
  | none, some _ => True
  | some _, none => True
  | some p, some q => p.1 = q.1 ∧ p.2 ≠ q.2

instance frAdjDec (n : ℕ) : DecidableRel (frAdj n) :=
  fun x y => by cases x <;> cases y <;> unfold frAdj <;> infer_instance

/-- The **friendship (windmill) graph** `F_n`: `n` triangles glued at a common central vertex. -/
def friendship (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Option (Fin n × Bool)) where
  Adj := frAdj n
  symm := by intro x y h; cases x <;> cases y <;> simp_all [frAdj]; tauto
  loopless := ⟨by rintro x h; cases x <;> simp_all [frAdj]⟩

instance (n : ℕ) : DecidableRel (friendship n).Adj := frAdjDec n

/-- The **friendship (windmill) graph** `F_n`: `n` triangles glued at a common central vertex. -/
def friendship (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Option (Fin n × Bool)) where
  Adj := frAdj n
  symm := by intro x y h; cases x <;> cases y <;> simp_all [frAdj]; tauto
  loopless := ⟨by rintro x h; cases x <;> simp_all [frAdj]⟩

instance (n : ℕ) : DecidableRel (friendship n).Adj := frAdjDec n

/-- The chromatic counting function `P(F_n, q)`: the number of proper colorings `V → Fin q` of the
friendship graph, i.e. the number of consistent assignments of `q` emotions. -/
def chromVal (n q : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter
    (fun c : Option (Fin n × Bool) → Fin q => ∀ x y, (friendship n).Adj x y → c x ≠ c y)).card

/-! ## Counting the colourings of one triangle -/

/-- For fixed centre colour `z` and one already-chosen outer colour `a ≠ z`, the remaining outer
colour has exactly `q - 2` choices (it must avoid both `z` and `a`). -/
theorem fiber_card (q : ℕ) (z a : Fin q) (h : a ≠ z) :
    Fintype.card {b : Fin q // b ≠ z ∧ b ≠ a} = q - 2 := by
  rw [Fintype.card_subtype]
  have heq : (univ.filter (fun b : Fin q => b ≠ z ∧ b ≠ a)) = ({z, a} : Finset (Fin q))ᶜ := by
    ext b; simp
  rw [heq, Finset.card_compl, Fintype.card_fin, Finset.card_pair h.symm]

/-- **Count for a single triangle.** Given the centre colour `z`, the ordered pairs of colours for
the two outer vertices of one triangle — both different from `z` and from each other — number
exactly `(q-1)(q-2)`. -/
theorem pairColors_card (q : ℕ) (z : Fin q) :
    Fintype.card {p : Fin q × Fin q // p.1 ≠ z ∧ p.2 ≠ z ∧ p.1 ≠ p.2} = (q - 1) * (q - 2) := by
  have e : {p : Fin q × Fin q // p.1 ≠ z ∧ p.2 ≠ z ∧ p.1 ≠ p.2}
      ≃ Σ a : {a : Fin q // a ≠ z}, {b : Fin q // b ≠ z ∧ b ≠ a.1} :=
    { toFun := fun p => ⟨⟨p.1.1, p.2.1⟩, ⟨p.1.2, p.2.2.1, fun hh => p.2.2.2 hh.symm⟩⟩
      invFun := fun s => ⟨(s.1.1, s.2.1), s.1.2, s.2.2.1, fun hh => s.2.2.2 hh.symm⟩
      left_inv := by rintro ⟨⟨a, b⟩, -⟩; rfl
      right_inv := by rintro ⟨⟨a, ha⟩, ⟨b, hb⟩⟩; rfl }
  rw [Fintype.card_congr e, Fintype.card_sigma]
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun a _ => fiber_card q z a.1 a.2)]
  rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, smul_eq_mul]
  have hz : Fintype.card {a : Fin q // a ≠ z} = q - 1 := by
    rw [Fintype.card_subtype]
    have : (univ.filter (fun a : Fin q => a ≠ z)) = ({z} : Finset (Fin q))ᶜ := by ext a; simp
    rw [this, Finset.card_compl, Fintype.card_fin, Finset.card_singleton]
  rw [hz]

/-! ## The colouring bijection -/

/-- **The structural bijection.** A proper colouring of `F_n` is exactly a choice of centre colour
`z : Fin q` together with, for each triangle `i`, an ordered pair of outer colours both avoiding `z`
and each other.  The forward map reads off the centre and each triangle's outer colours; the inverse
paints the centre with `z` and triangle `i`'s outer vertices with the recorded pair. -/
def frEquiv (n q : ℕ) :
    {c : Option (Fin n × Bool) → Fin q // ∀ x y, (friendship n).Adj x y → c x ≠ c y}
      ≃ Σ z : Fin q, (Fin n → {p : Fin q × Fin q // p.1 ≠ z ∧ p.2 ≠ z ∧ p.1 ≠ p.2}) where
  toFun := fun c =>
    ⟨c.1 none, fun i =>
      ⟨(c.1 (some (i, false)), c.1 (some (i, true))),
        c.2 (some (i, false)) none trivial,
        c.2 (some (i, true)) none trivial,
        c.2 (some (i, false)) (some (i, true)) ⟨rfl, Bool.false_ne_true⟩⟩⟩
  invFun := fun s =>
    ⟨fun v => match v with
      | none => s.1
      | some (i, b) => bif b then (s.2 i).1.2 else (s.2 i).1.1,
      by
        rintro x y h
        cases x with
        | none => cases y with
          | none => exact absurd h (by simp [friendship])
          | some p =>
            obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := p; have := (s.2 i).2; cases b <;> simp_all <;> tauto
        | some p =>
          obtain ⟨i, a⟩ := p
          cases y with
          | none => have := (s.2 i).2; cases a <;> simp_all
          | some p2 =>
            obtain ⟨j, b⟩ := p2
            obtain ⟨hij, hab⟩ : i = j ∧ a ≠ b := h
            subst hij
            have := (s.2 i).2.2.2
            cases a <;> cases b <;> simp_all [eq_comm]⟩
  left_inv := by
    rintro ⟨c, hc⟩; ext v
    cases v with
    | none => rfl
    | some p => obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := p; cases b <;> rfl
  right_inv := by rintro ⟨z, f⟩; congr 1

/-! ## The chromatic polynomial of the friendship graph -/

/-- **Main theorem.** The chromatic polynomial of the friendship graph `F_n` evaluated at `q` is
`q · ((q-1)(q-2))^n`: pick any of `q` emotions for the central person, then independently choose,
for each of the `n` triangles, an ordered pair of outer emotions both different from the centre and
from each other — `(q-1)(q-2)` choices per triangle. -/
theorem chromVal_friendship (n q : ℕ) :
    chromVal n q = q * ((q - 1) * (q - 2)) ^ n := by
  unfold chromVal
  rw [← Fintype.card_subtype, Fintype.card_congr (frEquiv n q), Fintype.card_sigma]
  have hcard : ∀ z : Fin q,
      Fintype.card (Fin n → {p : Fin q × Fin q // p.1 ≠ z ∧ p.2 ≠ z ∧ p.1 ≠ p.2})
        = ((q - 1) * (q - 2)) ^ n := by
    intro z; rw [Fintype.card_fun, pairColors_card, Fintype.card_fin]
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun z _ => hcard z), Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ,
    Fintype.card_fin, smul_eq_mul]

/-! ## Consequences -/

/-- **The six basic emotions.**  With a palette of the six basic emotions (happiness, sadness, anger,
fear, disgust, surprise), the friendship graph `F_n` has exactly `6 · 20^n` consistent emotion
assignments.  This is the closed form asserted by the "graph coloring with emotions" conjecture. -/
theorem friendship_chromVal_six (n : ℕ) : chromVal n 6 = 6 * 20 ^ n := by
  rw [chromVal_friendship]

/-- **The counting function is a colorability oracle.**  There is at least one consistent emotion
assignment with `q` emotions iff `P(F_n, q) > 0`. -/
theorem chromVal_pos_iff_colorable (n q : ℕ) :
    0 < chromVal n q ↔ (friendship n).Colorable q := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := Finset.card_pos.mp h
    exact ⟨SimpleGraph.Coloring.mk c (fun {x y} hxy => (Finset.mem_filter.mp hc).2 x y hxy)⟩
  · rintro ⟨c⟩
    exact Finset.card_pos.mpr
      ⟨c.toFun, Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨Finset.mem_univ _, fun x y hxy => c.valid hxy⟩⟩

/-- Three emotions always suffice for a friendship graph (`P(F_n, 3) = 3 · 2^n > 0`). -/
theorem friendship_colorable_three (n : ℕ) : (friendship n).Colorable 3 := by
  rw [← chromVal_pos_iff_colorable, chromVal_friendship]; norm_num

/-- The six basic emotions always suffice for a friendship graph. -/
theorem friendship_colorable_six (n : ℕ) : (friendship n).Colorable 6 :=
  (friendship_colorable_three n).mono (by norm_num)

/-- For `n ≥ 1`, two emotions never suffice: each triangle is a clique of three mutual friends, so
`P(F_n, 2) = 2 · 0^n = 0`. -/
theorem friendship_not_colorable_two {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) : ¬ (friendship n).Colorable 2 := by
  rw [← chromVal_pos_iff_colorable, chromVal_friendship]
  simp [zero_pow (show n ≠ 0 by omega)]

/-- **Chromatic number of the friendship graph.**  For `n ≥ 1`, `χ(F_n) = 3`: three emotions are
necessary (each triangle forces it) and sufficient.  Restricted to the emotional regime `k ≥ 3`,
this pins the emotional chromatic number of every nonempty friendship network to `3`, safely inside
the six-emotion window `[3, 6]`. -/
theorem friendship_chromaticNumber {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    (friendship n).chromaticNumber = 3 := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact chromaticNumber_le_iff_colorable.mpr (friendship_colorable_three n)
  · by_contra h
    rw [not_le] at h
    have hle : (friendship n).chromaticNumber ≤ 2 := Order.le_of_lt_succ h
    exact friendship_not_colorable_two hn (chromaticNumber_le_iff_colorable.mp hle)

end Catalog.Novelty.FriendshipChromaticPolynomial

concept.title: Matroid Minors and the Graph Theorem: Robertson-Seymour for Matroids
concept.concept_description: The Robertson-Seymour theorem states that the set of finite graphs is well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation: any infinite sequence of graphs contains two where one is a minor of the other. This implies that any minor-closed graph property is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. Conjecture: the same theorem holds for representable matroids over any finite field. Specifically, for any finite field F_q, the set of F_q-representable matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation. This would generalize the Robertson-Seymour theorem from graphs (F_2-representable matroids) to all finite fields. The conjecture is known to fail for general matroids (by the existence of infinite antichains of non-representable matroids), but for F_q-representable matroids with q <= 3, it is open. Conjecture: for F_3 (ternary matroids), the set of excluded minors for representability is finite. def minimalGens (U : Set α) : Set α := {x | x ∈ U ∧ ∀ y, y < x → y ∉ U}

lemma minimalGens_subset (U : Set α) : minimalGens U ⊆ U := fun _ hx => hx.1

/-- Minimal elements of a set form an antichain. -/
lemma isAntichain_minimalGens (U : Set α) :
    IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (minimalGens U) := by

import Mathlib

/-!
# A well-quasi-order bridge: forbidden minors and Dickson's lemma

This file isolates and proves the *order-theoretic engine* that is shared by two
areas which, on the surface, look unrelated:

* **Structural graph / matroid theory.**  The Robertson–Seymour theorem asserts
  that finite graphs are *well-quasi-ordered* (WQO) by the minor relation.  Its
  headline corollary is that every minor-closed family of graphs is described by
  a **finite** set of forbidden minors.  The conjectural extension of
  Robertson–Seymour to the class of `F_q`-representable matroids (the mission
  theme) would, via the very same engine, give a finite set of *excluded minors*
  for every minor-closed family of representable matroids.

* **Commutative algebra.**  Dickson's lemma says that `ℕ^k` is well-quasi-ordered
  by the coordinatewise (divisibility) order.  Its headline corollary is that
  every monomial ideal — equivalently every upward-closed set of exponent
  vectors — is **finitely generated**.

Both corollaries are instances of one abstract fact:

> In *any* partial order that is well-quasi-ordered by `≤`, every upper set is
> generated by its (finitely many) minimal elements, and dually every lower set
> is cut out by the (finitely many) minimal elements of its complement.

The "finitely many" is the crucial point and is exactly where WQO is used: an
antichain in a WQO is finite (`IsAntichain.finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered`), and the
minimal elements of any set form an antichain.

## Main results

* `WQOFiniteBasis.mem_iff_exists_minimalGen` — an upper set is exactly the up-set
  generated by its minimal elements.
* `WQOFiniteBasis.exists_finite_generating_family` — **finite generation of upper
  sets** (the abstract Dickson / Higman statement).
* `WQOFiniteBasis.exists_finite_forbidden_family` — **finite forbidden-obstruction
  characterization** of lower sets (the abstract Robertson–Seymour statement).
* `WQOFiniteBasis.dickson` — concrete specialization to `Fin k → ℕ`: every
  monomial-ideal-shaped upper set is finitely generated.
* `WQOFiniteBasis.robertson_seymour_of_wqo` — the forbidden-minor corollary for
  any WQO "minor order" on an abstract class of combinatorial objects.

The WQO vocabulary (`WellQuasiOrdered`, `IsAntichain.finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered`,
`WellQuasiOrdered.wellFounded`, and the instance `WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)`)
is taken from `Mathlib.Order.WellQuasiOrder`; the *bridge* lemmas below —
generation of upper sets by minimal elements and the forbidden-obstruction
characterization of lower sets — are the new contribution.
-/

open Set

namespace WQOFiniteBasis

variable {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α]

/-- The set of `≤`-minimal elements of a set `U`. -/
def minimalGens (U : Set α) : Set α := {x | x ∈ U ∧ ∀ y, y < x → y ∉ U}

lemma minimalGens_subset (U : Set α) : minimalGens U ⊆ U := fun _ hx => hx.1

/-- Minimal elements of a set form an antichain. -/
lemma isAntichain_minimalGens (U : Set α) :
    IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (minimalGens U) := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  exact fun h => hy.2 x (lt_of_le_of_ne h hxy) hx.1

/-- In a well-quasi-order, the set of minimal elements of any set is finite:
it is an antichain, and antichains are finite in a WQO. -/
lemma minimalGens_finite (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop)) :
    (minimalGens U).Finite :=
  (isAntichain_minimalGens U).finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered hwqo

/-- In a well-quasi-order every element of a set dominates a minimal element of
that set (via well-foundedness of `<`). -/
lemma exists_minimalGen_le (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    {x : α} (hx : x ∈ U) : ∃ g ∈ minimalGens U, g ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ : ∃ g ∈ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x}, ∀ z ∈ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x}, ¬(z < g) := by
    convert (WellFounded.has_min _ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x} ⟨x, hx, le_rfl⟩) using 1
    convert hwqo.wellFounded using 1
    grind +suggestions
  exact ⟨g, ⟨hg.1.1, fun z hz hz' => hg.2 z ⟨hz', hz.le.trans hg.1.2⟩ hz⟩, hg.1.2⟩

/-- An upper set of a well-quasi-order equals the up-set generated by its minimal
elements. -/
theorem mem_iff_exists_minimalGen (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (hU : IsUpperSet U) (x : α) :
    x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ minimalGens U, g ≤ x := by
  constructor
  · exact fun hx => exists_minimalGen_le U hwqo hx
  · exact fun ⟨g, hg, hgx⟩ => hU hgx (minimalGens_subset U hg)

/-- **Finite generation of upper sets.**  Abstractly this is the content of
Dickson's lemma / the Higman finite-basis property: in a well-quasi-order, every
upward-closed set is generated by a finite set of elements below it. -/
theorem exists_finite_generating_family
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (U : Set α) (hU : IsUpperSet U) :
    ∃ G : Set α, G.Finite ∧ G ⊆ U ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ G, g ≤ x :=
  ⟨minimalGens U, minimalGens_finite U hwqo, minimalGens_subset U,
    fun x => mem_iff_exists_minimalGen U hwqo hU x⟩

/-- **Finite forbidden-obstruction characterization of lower sets.**  Abstractly
this is the content of the Robertson–Seymour corollary: in a well-quasi-order,
every downward-closed (minor-closed) set `S` is described by a finite family `B`
of "forbidden" elements, in the sense that `x ∈ S` iff no forbidden element lies
below `x`.  The family `B` is the set of minimal elements of the complement. -/
theorem exists_finite_forbidden_family
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (S : Set α) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ B : Set α, B.Finite ∧ B ⊆ Sᶜ ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hB₁, hB₂, hB₃⟩ := exists_finite_generating_family hwqo Sᶜ hS.compl
  simp_all only [Set.subset_def, Set.mem_compl_iff]
  grind

/-- **Robertson–Seymour corollary, abstract form.**  If a class of combinatorial
objects (graphs, or `F_q`-representable matroids) is well-quasi-ordered by its
"minor" order, then every minor-closed property is characterized by a *finite*
set of forbidden minors.  This is exactly `exists_finite_forbidden_family`, stated
in the language of the mission. -/
theorem robertson_seymour_of_wqo
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (S : Set α) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ forbidden : Set α, forbidden.Finite ∧
      ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ forbidden, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hBfin, _, hB⟩ := exists_finite_forbidden_family hwqo S hS
  exact ⟨B, hBfin, hB⟩

/-! ## Concrete bridge: Dickson's lemma on `Fin k → ℕ`

We now instantiate the abstract engine on the exponent lattice `Fin k → ℕ`,
where `≤` is coordinatewise (equivalently monomial divisibility).  Mathlib
provides the instance `WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)`, so the abstract results
apply verbatim, yielding Dickson's lemma: every monomial-ideal-shaped upper set
is finitely generated. -/

/-- `ℕ` is well-quasi-ordered by `≤`. -/
theorem wqo_nat : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : ℕ → ℕ → Prop) :=
  (inferInstance : WellQuasiOrderedLE ℕ).wqo

/-- The exponent lattice `Fin k → ℕ` is well-quasi-ordered by the coordinatewise
order — this is Dickson's lemma. -/
theorem wqo_fin_pi (k : ℕ) :
    WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : (Fin k → ℕ) → (Fin k → ℕ) → Prop) :=
  (inferInstance : WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)).wqo

/-- **Dickson's lemma, finite-generation form.**  Every upward-closed set of
exponent vectors in `ℕ^k` (equivalently, every monomial ideal) is finitely
generated by finitely many minimal exponent vectors. -/
theorem dickson (k : ℕ) (U : Set (Fin k → ℕ)) (hU : IsUpperSet U) :
    ∃ G : Set (Fin k → ℕ), G.Finite ∧ G ⊆ U ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ G, g ≤ x :=
  exists_finite_generating_family (wqo_fin_pi k) U hU

/-- Concrete forbidden-minor characterization on `ℕ` itself: every downward-closed
set of naturals is cut out by a finite forbidden set. -/
theorem forbidden_family_nat (S : Set ℕ) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ B : Set ℕ, B.Finite ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hBfin, _, hB⟩ := exists_finite_forbidden_family wqo_nat S hS
  exact ⟨B, hBfin, hB⟩

end WQOFiniteBasis

# Computational evidence

The theorem proved here (`Catalog/Novelty/ExcludedMinors/WellQuasiOrderFiniteBasis.lean`)
is the order-theoretic engine behind two finiteness phenomena:

* **Robertson–Seymour** — a minor-closed family is cut out by *finitely many*
  forbidden minors;
* **Dickson's lemma** — a monomial ideal (upper set of exponent vectors in `ℕ^k`)
  has *finitely many* minimal generators.

Being a universally quantified identity about well-quasi-orders, it is not a
numerical conjecture; the "evidence" is that the finiteness it predicts is
observed in every small instance, and that no counterexample can exist because
the finiteness is forced by antichain-finiteness in a WQO.

## 1. Small cases of the forbidden-family theorem on `ℕ`

For `S ⊆ ℕ` a lower set (initial segment), `exists_finite_forbidden_family`
produces `B = minimal elements of Sᶜ`:

| lower set `S`            | complement `Sᶜ`   | forbidden set `B` | size |
|--------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|------|
| `∅`                      | `ℕ`               | `{0}`             | 1    |
| `{0}`                    | `{1,2,3,...}`     | `{1}`             | 1    |
| `{0,1,...,n-1}`          | `{n,n+1,...}`     | `{n}`             | 1    |
| `ℕ` (all)                | `∅`               | `∅`               | 0    |

Every proper lower set of `ℕ` is `{x | x < n}` and is forbidden by the single
element `n`; the "all" set has empty forbidden family. Finite in every case. ✓

## 2. Small cases of Dickson's lemma on `ℕ^2`

Minimal generators of upper sets `U ⊆ ℕ^2` (monomial ideals):

| upper set `U` (as `x ≥ g` union)        | minimal generators `G`      | size |
|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------|------|
| `⟨2,0⟩ ≤ x  or  ⟨0,3⟩ ≤ x`              | `{(2,0),(0,3)}`             | 2    |
| `⟨1,1⟩ ≤ x`                             | `{(1,1)}`                   | 1    |
| `⟨3,0⟩,⟨2,1⟩,⟨0,2⟩ ≤ x`                 | `{(3,0),(2,1),(0,2)}`       | 3    |
| `ℕ^2 \ {(0,0)}` (everything but origin) | `{(1,0),(0,1)}`             | 2    |

Each monomial ideal has a finite minimal generating antichain, as Dickson's
lemma guarantees. ✓ (These match the standard "staircase" pictures of monomial
ideals.)

## 3. The mission's excluded-minor count (context)

The mission text lists the ternary (GF(3)) excluded minors as `F_7`, `F_7*`, and
the non-Pappus matroid. The *established* theorem (Bixby; Seymour; Kahn) is that
the excluded minors for GF(3)-representability are exactly the **five** matroids

    U_{2,5},  U_{3,5},  F_7,  F_7*,  P_8 .

The exact list is not what our Lean theorem asserts; what our theorem captures is
the structural reason such a list is **finite at all**: GF(3)-representable
matroids are (conjecturally, and by the Geelen–Gerards–Whittle program) WQO under
minors, and *any* WQO minor order forces every minor-closed class — in particular
the class of representable matroids — to have a finite forbidden-minor set. The
finite cardinality 5 above is one confirmed data point of this finiteness.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

No counterexample is possible: `exists_finite_forbidden_family` and `dickson` are
proved in Lean with only the axioms `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound`
(verified by `#print axioms`). The finiteness cannot fail in any WQO because an
antichain in a WQO is finite (`IsAntichain.finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered`), and the
forbidden/generating family is always an antichain
(`isAntichain_minimalGens`).
